idiom_name: throwing init + guard over let stored properties (definite initialization); fileprivate init + co-located Essence factory when validation is shared
implementation_notes: Swift absorbs the Essence/CreationTarget split into its own construction machinery: a throwing initializer on the target validates every compulsory property with guard/throw before self is fully initialized, and because the compiler enforces definite initialization, no instance exists at all unless every check passed - the always-valid invariant is carried by the language, not by a second class. let stored properties give the compulsory-immutable-after-creation guarantee natively, and defining any custom init suppresses the synthesized memberwise initializer (which is internal at best anyway), which is exactly the restricted-constructor requirement. The classic two-class form stays justified when validation needs shared context or one bundle feeds several related targets: declare a fileprivate init on the target and keep a co-located ContractEssence type with validate() throws for early feedback and create() throws -> Contract in the same file (Swift has no friend, but fileprivate init is the friend/package-private equivalent for co-located types). Failable init? is the non-throwing flavor for the many cases where an absent value - not an error - is the honest result (e.g. init?(rawValue:)).
pitfalls: Memberwise backdoor: a struct without any custom init gets a synthesized memberwise initializer, so within the same module Contract(customer:supplier:startDate:) compiles and produces an unvalidated instance - always define an explicit init (which suppresses synthesis) or make the compulsory properties private.

Decodable synthesis bypasses validation: the compiler-generated init(from:) assigns stored properties directly, so a Contract decoded from JSON can be invalid - write init(from:) manually and delegate to the validating initializer, or revalidate at the decoding boundary.

Force-unwrap conversion: callers who try! or postfix-! a failable init? turn failed validation into a deferred runtime crash at the unwrap site instead of a handled error at creation - prefer throwing init with typed errors and reserve init! for Objective-C bridge interop.

Default property values re-open the invalid door: var startDate: Date = .distantPast keeps a mutable property that can be assigned an invalid value later; keep compulsory properties let so the invariant is compile-enforced.

Overriding a failable superclass initializer with a nonfailable subclass initializer silently widens the validity guarantee - the subclass constructs even when the superclass validation rejects the input.
